assessment.nobel_worthiness: Topological insulators opened a new class of quantum matter in which band topology, not symmetry breaking, protects boundary states. The Kane-Mele quantum spin Hall proposal and its realisation in HgTe wells led to a large body of materials and spectroscopy work, including ARPES and first-principles band-structure confirmation. This is the kind of verified new state of matter in real materials that I value most.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele supplied the theoretical framework (Z2 invariant, spin-orbit-driven quantum spin Hall state). Molenkamp's group gave the first transport observation in HgTe/CdTe wells, following the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction. Other theorists (Bernevig, Zhang, Fu, Moore, Balents) and the 3D topological insulator experiments (Hasan) are credited elsewhere, so a three-person configuration will leave some claims unaddressed, but Kane, Mele and Molenkamp are defensible.
assessment.maturity: Nearly two decades of independent theory and experiment, with many material realisations and ARPES confirmation. Recognition is timely, arguably overdue.
uncertainties: The attribution is crowded: Bernevig, Zhang, Fu, Hasan and others have strong claims that the supplied credit list does not include.
I am recalling the chronology of the HgTe prediction and experiment from memory and have not verified the details.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene showed that a simple twist produces flat bands, correlated insulators and superconductivity in a clean, tunable system. It created the moire materials field and is a clear example of theory predicting and experiment confirming a new quantum regime. It also fits my interest in a stable 2D crystal revealing unexpected physics.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted the flat bands at the magic angle, and Jarillo-Herrero's group observed correlated insulators and superconductivity (2018). Cao's role as first author of the experiments is not captured in the credit list, and other groups also contributed to related work. The theory-plus-experiment pairing is natural, though the allocation is not fully clean.
assessment.maturity: Experimental reproduction by many groups is strong, and DFT and tight-binding modelling broadly agree on the flat bands. The microscopic origin of the superconductivity is still debated, and the field is young, so timing is somewhat early but acceptable.
uncertainties: The pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is unresolved.
Sample-to-sample variation is large, and the roles of Cao and other contributors are not represented in the credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance and its enhancement in MgO junctions turned spin-dependent tunnelling into the basis of modern read heads and MRAM. The discovery rests on spin-polarised tunnelling physics, with symmetry-filtering of Bloch states that first-principles theory (Butler, Mathon and others) explained quantitatively. It is a case where measured spectra and calculation agree and where the technological impact is large.
assessment.attribution: Miyazaki and Moodera independently reported large room-temperature TMR in 1995, and Parkin's group and Yuasa/Djayaprawira demonstrated MgO coherent tunnelling in 2004. Yuasa, Djayaprawira and the theorists Butler and Mathon have claims outside the supplied credit list. The three credited names are reasonable but leave real priority questions.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with two decades of commercial deployment and good agreement between theory and experiment. Timing is good, though the GMR prize of 2007 may make some members feel the area has already been honoured.
uncertainties: Credit for MgO coherent tunnelling is split among several experimental groups and theorists.
Possible overlap with the 2007 GMR prize may weigh against it.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamical mean-field theory gave a controlled non-perturbative treatment of strongly correlated electrons, giving a quantitative account of the Mott transition and, combined with DFT (DFT+DMFT), predictions for real materials. It is conceptually original and widely used, with direct links to spectroscopy and to my own field of electronic-structure theory.
assessment.attribution: Metzner and Vollhardt's infinite-dimension limit, and Georges and Kotliar's mapping onto the Anderson impurity problem, together made the framework. Müller-Hartmann and others also made early contributions, and Metzner is not in the credited list. The three names are a plausible configuration but the original lattice-limit insight is shared with Metzner.
assessment.maturity: More than 30 years of use across correlated-materials physics, with agreement with photoemission and optical spectra in many systems. The accuracy of DMFT for specific materials depends on the impurity solver and the double-counting treatment, so reproducibility across codes is not as clean as for plain DFT.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees this as a method rather than a discovery.
Metzner's contribution is not in the supplied credit list.
Reliability depends on the impurity solver and double-counting choices.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock, built on the magic-wavelength proposal, reached fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 and enabled tests of fundamental physics and relativistic geodesy. It is a clear metrological advance with large lasting impact.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and demonstrated the first Sr lattice clock. Ye's group pushed the accuracy and stability to the current record levels. The two-person allocation is clean, though Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom and others did notable experimental work.
assessment.maturity: Many independent clocks agree at the 1e-18 level, and international comparisons are underway. The redefinition of the second is still pending, but the recognition would be timely.
uncertainties: Some members may see this as precision engineering over new physics.
The thorium nuclear clock may later compete for the same laureate slot (Ye).

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realise clean Hubbard models, with the superfluid-to-Mott transition and later quantum gas microscopes providing direct access to correlated many-body states. As a theorist of lattice models I find the quantum-simulator idea attractive, as long as the work yields reliable new physics.
assessment.attribution: Jaksch and Zoller's proposal, Greiner, Mandel, Hansch and Bloch's Mott experiment, and Esslinger's fermionic work are all key. Any three-person prize would exclude some of Esslinger, Jaksch, Hänsch and Kasevich. The list I chose reflects the theory-plus-experiment pairing, which is arguable.
assessment.maturity: Highly mature and replicated across many groups. The Bose-Einstein condensation prize of 2001 and the 2012 and 2018 AMO prizes make some AMO-adjacent areas look partly honoured already.
uncertainties: Attribution is spread over many leaders, so any three-person set is contestable.
Many of the simulations are not yet beyond the reach of classical methods.
The overlap with earlier cold-atom prizes.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum anomalous Hall effect gives quantised Hall conductance with no applied field in a magnetic topological insulator. It joins magnetism and topology, and it is a clean demonstration of a theoretical prediction. Magnetic topological insulators fall near my own expertise.
assessment.attribution: Fang and Dai, with colleagues, predicted the effect in Cr- or Fe-doped Bi2Te3-family materials in 2010. Xue's group observed it in Cr-doped (Bi,Sb)2Te3 in 2013. Chang, Haldane's earlier model, and Yu and Zhang have notable claims as well. The credited trio is a natural theory-experiment pairing.
assessment.maturity: Independently reproduced (including at Stanford and Penn State), but the quantisation temperatures are low and the materials remain inhomogeneous. It is somewhat early compared with topological insulators and would more naturally follow that prize.
uncertainties: The operating temperature is far below the ideal.
The Haldane and Chang contributions are not fully reflected in the credit list.
Whether it would be recognised separately from topological insulators.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The 1988 discovery of conductance quantisation in ballistic point contacts was a clean demonstration of quantum transport in a mesoscopic device, and it became the basis for quantum point contacts and later spin and quantum-dot experiments. It is simple, original, and has been reproduced many times.
assessment.attribution: Two groups, van Wees and colleagues in Delft/Philips and Wharam and colleagues at the Cavendish with Pepper, reported the effect at nearly the same time. The credited names cover both groups, though one could argue about others, and the theoretical contributions (Landauer formalism, Büttiker) are not among them.
assessment.maturity: Very mature and thoroughly confirmed. The discovery is almost forty years old, so recognition would be late, which I regard as a possible weakness for a prize and also a sign that the work has stood the test of time. The 1985 and 1998 quantum Hall prizes cover neighbouring ground.
uncertainties: Late timing, and possible concern about a lack of recent momentum.
Landauer-Büttiker theory is not credited.
Partial overlap with the earlier quantum Hall prizes.
